newsitem.title: USA: Clinton gets assurances on Hong Kong from Chinese.
newsitem.headline: Clinton gets assurances on Hong Kong from Chinese.

text.p: Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen assured President Bill Clinton on Wednesday that Hong Kong would retain autonomy under Chinese control, and Clinton said he hoped this reflected China's policy.

Clinton and Qian met privately in the Oval Office in what U.S. officials said was a broad discussion of the U.S.-Chinese agenda including human rights, Hong Kong, the spread of weapons of mass destruction and trade issues.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry said the two spoke only briefly about allegations that China attempted to influence last year's U.S. election by funnelling donations to the Clinton campaign. This part of the discussion lasted "probably about 30 seconds," McCurry said; Clinton raised the issue and Qian repeated Chinese denials of any such effort.

Clinton, talking briefly to reporters after the meeting, said Qian assured him China intended to observe the terms of its 1984 agreement with Britain guaranteeing Hong Kong's autonomy once it reverts to Chinese rule on July 1.
"I was quite satisfied with what was said and I certainly hope that it will reflect Chinese policy," Clinton said.

The United States has grown increasingly concerned about Hong Kong as the changeover draws near, with many critics charging that preparatory steps by Beijing are eroding democracy and basic freedoms in the longtime British colony.
Martin Lee, Hong Kong's leading pro-democracy activist, was in Washington last week urging the Americans to press Beijing strongly to preserve Hong Kong's rights and freedoms.

U.S. House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich warned China on Wednesday its handling of the takeover might damage its chances of retaining Most Favoured Nation (MFN) trading status with the United States.

He said in a speech at the Paul H. Nitze School of Advanced International Studies that he favoured legislation proposed in Congress to limit MFN status for China to between three and six months. "There would be serious long-term damage to our relations" if Beijing did not live up to its agreement to allow democratic freedoms in Hong Kong when it takes control of the British colony on July 1, he said.
Gingrich said he would endorse either of two proposals made in the House, one extending MFN status for three months, one extending it for three to six months, to see how China deals with Hong Kong.
McCurry, asked about the idea, said the current annual review for China "works satisfactorily" and was sceptical of Gingrich's idea. "We'll just see if it goes anywhere."
Clinton, who supports a policy of active engagement with China, favours renewal of the favourable trade status for China for another year but faces some opposition in Congress.

White House spokesman David Johnson said much of the discussion between Clinton and Qian was on plans for an autumn summit between Clinton and Chinese President Jiang Zemin. It is to be in Washington either before or after the annual summit of the Asian Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, which this year will be in Vancouver, British Columbia.

As part of those plans, Johnson said the two leaders had a "quite civil discussion" about Chinese human rights practices with hopes of being able to make progress on the issue at the summit. "I think the Chinese share the idea of trying to make progress on human rights. I think where we have work to do is to define mutually what that progress is," he said.

He said the two leaders also discussed U.S. concerns about weapons of mass destruction falling into the hands of rogue states. "They talked about non-proliferation and the need to work together in order to limit proliferation to areas of instability, including Iran."
